MONOLITH / FIELD MANUAL

Paper rises.
Concrete has limits.

Reach 12 developed plots and 6,000 CR of combined equity. Survive at least 12 settlements with a solvent bank and no failed subsidiaries.

01 / PRODUCE

Build a foundation.

Infrastructure costs 40 reserves, adds 4 utility capacity to its district, and earns 12 reserves each day from a finite outside treasury. Every fourth day, district capacity falls by 2 for maintenance.

02 / REVALUE

Make the paper rise.

Select the starter subsidiary, then revalue its 100 CR land to 400 CR. Assets and revaluation equity rise together. Further revaluations triple value, up to three rounds. Each round adds 2 utility demand.

03 / LEVERAGE

Borrow against the future.

Select a subsidiary with unpledged equity, choose Debt link, and click an adjacent empty plot. Each 100 CR loan creates a new subsidiary and 100 CR of deposits. Each sponsor can support floor(equity ÷ 100) active links.

04 / SETTLE

Keep the system liquid.

Settle day pays infrastructure income, tests utility loads, then nets supplier transfers to an outside bank against service payments back to the parent. Under-supplied land loses 35% of value. Only the net balance moves in reserves. Supplier payments to the bank itself reduce deposits and increase bank earnings.

When the concrete fractures

Negative subsidiary equity must be resolved: absorb debt through a parent write-off, or isolate the plot through foreclosure. Both can reduce bank capital. Below 8% bank capital / risk-weighted assets, new credit freezes. Bank equity at or below zero causes systemic collapse. A liquidity freeze pauses clearing; recover by selling infrastructure or waiting a recovery day for its reserve income. Recovery days also apply infrastructure stress.

Accounting assumptions & controls

This is an accounting simulation, not a claim that projected capacity legally permits unrestricted revaluation or lending. The parent is a deposit-taking bank. External land sellers hold its deposits and clear to a separate bank. Daily settlement demand is modeled from outstanding supplier balances and cross-district links, with fixed incoming service fees; it is a game rule. Same-bank customer transfers do not require reserves. All loans and fixed assets have a simplified 100% risk weight; reserves have 0%. Subsidiary revaluation surplus is excluded from parent regulatory capital. Intercompany balances remain in the combined display; “All books” shows a consolidated view and the external counterparties. Base money is conserved across bank, treasury, supplier and outside-bank accounts.
